conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for making time for this visit. I’m Dana, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’m here simply to see how you’re doing in these first weeks of new motherhood.

We’ll use a short, well-validated questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**. It’s just 10 questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days; it helps us pick up on signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up after birth, and it includes one question about self-harm so we can keep you safe. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me you might hurt yourself or your baby, and then we’ll bring in extra support together.

There are no right or wrong answers, and you don’t need to explain anything unless you want to. When you’re ready, I’ll ask the first question, and we’ll go from there. How does that sound?

To begin:  
In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

*shifts in the chair, eyes a little glassy*

Honestly? I... I used to laugh all the time. My husband will make jokes like he always did, and I know they're funny, but... it's like I'm too tired to even smile. Last night he tried to make me laugh about how the baby projectile-pooped on his shirt, and I just... couldn't. I felt bad because I knew it was funny, but it felt like too much effort to laugh.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*quietly*  
No… not really. Most of the week it’s felt pretty hard to laugh.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*wrings hands in lap*

Not really... I used to get excited about little things like my morning coffee or taking a walk, but now even when I plan them I just feel... flat. Like, my sister asked me to go get our nails done tomorrow and I said yes because I know I *should* want to go, but inside I felt nothing. Maybe a little dread about having to pretend I'm okay for an hour.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods slowly, eyes dropping to the floor*

Yeah... I do that a lot. Yesterday the baby wouldn't stop crying for like an hour, and I kept thinking it must be something I'm doing wrong. Maybe I'm not feeding him right, or I'm not holding him the way he needs. When he finally settled, instead of feeling relieved, I just kept thinking how I'm probably messing him up already. My partner says I'm too hard on myself, but... what if he's only crying because I'm not good at this.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*nods, pressing my lips together*

Yes… pretty much every day. Like, I’ll sit down to feed her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s not getting enough milk, even though the pediatrician says she’s gaining fine. Last night I kept checking if she was breathing—three, four times. I know it sounds crazy, but I can’t shake the feeling something awful is about to happen, even when everything looks okay.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*clasps hands tightly in lap, voice shaky*

A few times… yeah. Yesterday I was just folding laundry while she napped and suddenly my chest got tight, like I couldn’t get air. My heart was pounding so hard I thought I might pass out. I kept telling myself nothing was wrong—the house was quiet, she’s safe—but it felt like something terrible was about to happen. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky the rest of the afternoon.
Things have been getting on top of me

*exhales slowly, shoulders sagging*

Yes… most days it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. Dishes pile up, the baby needs changing, I haven’t showered, and I just stand in the kitchen staring, paralyzed. I’ll think, “I can’t do all this,” and my chest gets heavy. I manage—eventually—but it feels like I’m barely treading water, and the next wave is always right there.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*looks away, voice small*

Yeah… I’ll lie down exhausted, but my mind just keeps spinning. I keep replaying every little thing I did that day—did I hold her right, did I miss a sign something was wrong, am I already failing her? By the time I finally drift off, she’s usually ready for another feed, and then I’m wide awake again, feeling miserable and guilty for being miserable.
I have felt sad or miserable

*nods slowly, eyes filling*

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like a gray cloud that won’t lift. I’ll be feeding her and tears just start rolling down my face for no clear reason. I keep thinking I should feel happy—she’s healthy, I wanted her so much—but instead I feel empty and weepy. I find myself crying in the shower so no one sees.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*voice cracks, tears welling*

Yes… it’s happened a few times just since yesterday. I’ll be changing her diaper or folding onesies and suddenly I’m sobbing. Not little tears—big, ugly crying that makes my chest hurt. I feel like I’m failing at the one thing I’m supposed to be doing, and the tears just come whether I want them or not.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly, eyes wide*

No… no, I haven’t thought about that. I feel overwhelmed and sad, but I would never want to leave her. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

You've shared that the past week has felt overwhelmingly heavy: joy and laughter feel out of reach, daily tasks seem paralysing, and a constant gray cloud of sadness, guilt and worry has settled over what you hoped would be a happy time. You cry easily, feel you're failing your baby, wake with racing thoughts, and even experienced a sudden wave of panic, yet you emphatically want to stay here for your child.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient explicitly states "not really" and describes difficulty laughing most of the week, aligning with "Not at all".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure and emotional flatness, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent self-blame for baby's crying, feeling she's "messing him up" and inadequacy as a mother, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily, intrusive, irrational worries about infant feeding and safety, indicating severe anxiety occurring 'very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete panic-like episode with physical symptoms (tight chest, pounding heart) and catastrophic thoughts, occurring "a few times"—maps to "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent daily overwhelm, inability to initiate tasks, and feeling paralyzed—aligns with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly racing thoughts, inability to fall asleep, and recurrent waking, indicating sleep difficulty 'most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying daily, feeling empty and weepy, and spontaneous tears multiple times per day, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense crying episodes that occur spontaneously and uncontrollably, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score of 26/30 far exceeds the ≥14 threshold indicating probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. Symptoms map to <med>DSM-5 criteria</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), significant weight/appetite change not assessed here but reported emotional eating changes possible, sleep disruption, psychomotor agitation (hand-wringing, tearfulness), fatigue, feelings of worthlessness/excessive guilt (<quote>I'm already messing him up</quote>), diminished concentration and recurrent thoughts of death ruled out by negative Item 10. Symptoms began after birth, occur daily, cause clinically significant distress and functional impairment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary-care provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med>
2. Begin evidence-based psychotherapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy) that specialises in <med>postpartum depression</med>
3. Discuss starting antidepressant medication compatible with breastfeeding if no contraindications
4. Plan daily 15-minute support call/text with partner/friend to monitor mood and safety
5. Encourage 20-30 minutes of daylight walk or gentle exercise when baby sleeps
6. Promote 4-hour uninterrupted sleep block once nightly-partner or family handle feeding shift
7. Provide emergency resources: 24/7 Postpartum Support International helpline and local urgent mental-health number
8. Re-screen EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress after interventions
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant ≈ weeks–months old)  
Date: [today]  
Screener: [name], Licensed Mental Health Professional  

I. Responses to 10-item EPDS-based interview  
A1–A10 indicate:  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily crying spells  
- Marked guilt / self-blame re parenting competence  
- Generalized anxiety, nocturnal rumination, panic-type episode  
- Overwhelm / “drowning” with routine tasks  
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood (not solely infant demands)  
- Denies self-harm ideation (A10)  

II. Observed signs during interview  
Psychomotor slowing, tearfulness, hand-wringing, voice quavering; congruent depressed affect.  

III. Endorsement pattern (frequency)  
- Anhedonia / sadness: daily (A1, A2, A8, A9)  
- Guilt / self-blame: most days (A3)  
- Anxiety / panic: daily, one acute episode (A4, A5)  
- Overwhelm: most days (A6)  
- Insomnia: 6–7 nights/week (A7)  
- Crying: daily (A9)  

IV. Screening significance  
Score consistent with probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; meets threshold for further evaluation for postpartum depression and possible panic spectrum symptoms. Denies suicidal intent. No self-harm plan or intent reported.  

V. Risk factors identified  
- Infant-care guilt (“I’m already messing him up”)  
- Panic-type episode while infant asleep  
- Nighttime mood-linked insomnia  
- Social withdrawal / masking distress (crying in shower)  

VI. Safety  
No active suicidal ideation; no self-harm thoughts; no protective concerns voiced. Continue routine safety monitoring.  

VII. Next steps recommended  
Comprehensive clinical interview, formal EPDS scoring, referral to reproductive psychiatry / therapy services, psychoeducation, safety-planning, support-system activation.
